short: A new CTC sentence decoder, but one corpus and one run make it standard; the comparisons break: an 86.4% word-level HMM baseline, a 10-minute panel, silent dictation untested.
position: LipNet [@assael2016lipnet] changes one component, the decoder (M06): spatiotemporal convolutions, Bi-GRUs and a character CTC loss in one model. The design is new, since none of the 67 sentence-level lip-reading studies first public before 2016-11 names a CTC or attention decoder and 41 name hidden Markov models, but the evidence supports only standard: one corpus, one run per split, no seed or interval, and an ablation that puts the gain in the 3D front end rather than in CTC. The headline comparisons do not hold: the 86.4% "state-of-the-art" is a video-only accuracy from speaker-dependent word HMMs with the full GRID grammar [@gergen2016turbo], so the 2.8x claim crosses task level, split and decoder constraint, and the "experienced human lipreaders" are three hearing-impaired students given ten minutes of annotated video. Silent dictation is named as the use that demands video only, yet no silent articulation is tested, though overt-trained lip-video recognisers lose accuracy on it [@petridis2018visual]. The lasting contribution is the GRID protocol (M12), now followed by 54 unseen-speaker and 41 overlapped-speaker studies, but its single-run reporting falls short of the speaker spread and significance test given by the study it reimplements [@wand2016lipreading].
